On the morning the town’s clocks began running backward, Mara was late for work.

She noticed first in the kitchen. The second hand on the wall clock moved from twelve to eleven to ten. She tapped the glass. It continued. On her phone, the time read 7:43, then 7:42.

Outside, the baker was standing in his doorway, holding a tray of rolls.

“Did you see?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Are we supposed to open?”

Mara looked down the street. The florist had put out her buckets of flowers. A bus passed with three passengers aboard, all staring at their phones.

“I would,” Mara said.

At the town hall, the clocks were going backward too, which was unfortunate because Mara’s job was to issue parking permits, and the permit software required a date and time. When she tried to enter one, the screen displayed an error message: **EXPIRATION CANNOT PRECEDE ISSUE.**

She called the software company. After a long wait, a man named Dennis answered.

“Have you tried restarting?” he asked.

“I’ve tried everything except going home.”

“Let me check with my supervisor.”

Mara put the phone on speaker and listened to a recording of a piano playing the same eight bars. Across the counter, an elderly woman waited for her permit, resting both hands on a walking stick.

“Would you like to sit?” Mara asked.

“No, thank you. I’ve been sitting all morning.”

They listened to the piano.

“My husband used to play,” the woman said. “Not well enough for recordings.”

“What did he play?”

“Mostly things he made up. He was very fond of one tune in particular. It went on so long you could leave the room, make tea, come back, and he’d still be playing it.”

“Was it good?”

“No,” said the woman. “But he was cheerful.”

Dennis returned to the line. His supervisor had recommended a full system reset.

“What happens to the permits we’ve already issued?” Mara asked.

“They should remain in the database.”

“Should?”

There was a pause. “Probably.”

Mara decided against the reset. She took a blank permit from the drawer, filled it out by hand, and stamped it with the town seal. The ink came out faintly purple.

“There,” she said.

The woman examined it. “Will it be valid?”

“If anyone asks, tell them I said so.”

The woman tucked the permit into her handbag and thanked her.

By noon—or what would ordinarily have been noon—the clocks were still running backward, but the town had settled into its day. The baker sold out of rolls. The bus completed its route. Children came home from school with worksheets explaining how the hands of a clock were *supposed* to move.

At four, Mara closed the permit office and walked home. The baker was sweeping flour from his step.

“Good day?” she asked.

“Not bad,” he said. “I opened.”

That evening, the clock on Mara’s kitchen wall stopped at 11:59. Its second hand rested there for a moment, then moved to twelve, one, two.

Mara watched it for a while. Then she set it to the right time and went to make dinner.
